faq.q: Will the ingredient list and nutrition panel look right?
faq.a: Do not rely on the image for that. Small print may not match the real package. Allergens, ingredients, and nutrition facts should always come from the real label.

faq.q: Can I show a pour if I only have a photo of the can?
faq.a: Yes. Upload the can or paste a product link, then describe the glass, the ice, and the color of the liquid. Name the texture in plain words so the pour stays close to the real drink.

faq.q: How long should a food clip be?
faq.a: 6 or 10 seconds covers one pour or one bite. Use 15 seconds for two moments, or 30 seconds for a longer serve. A 6-second clip is 24 credits, 10 seconds is 40, 15 is 60, and 30 is 120. A failed job returns its credits.

faq.q: Should I spray the can for a cold look?
faq.a: No. Ask for condensation in the description, then photograph the dry can in side window light with fingerprints wiped off.

faq.q: Can I run the clips as paid food and drink ads?
faq.a: Yes. The download has no watermark, and you can use it in paid ads. Leave nutrition, allergen, and ingredient text on the real package.

faq.q: Do I need a creator or a filming kitchen?
faq.a: Not for these clips. Pick a generated presenter, or let the hands come from your package photo. A real tasting, or a recipe you must show exactly, still needs a real shoot.

faq.q: Which video shapes can I use?
faq.a: Video shapes are a tall phone video (9:16), a square (1:1), a wide video (16:9), 4:3, or 3:4. 4:3 is a bit wider than a square. 3:4 is a bit taller than a square. A tall 9:16 fits a phone feed. A square photo fits many listings.

faq.q: What should the scene keep visible?
faq.a: Keep the package shape and the main label area recognizable, and end on the full product when you can. Do not ask the clip to invent a flavor that is not in the photo.

faq.q: Can a drink clip include a voice, captions, and another language?
faq.a: Yes. The clip can include a spoken line and captions, and the same pour can be made again in another language. Allergens stay on the real package. A failed job returns its credits.
